cards.front: In the model for this lesson, who does the copying when a bacterium multiplies, and who does it when a virus multiplies?
cards.back: A bacterium copies itself. A virus is copied by a host cell, the living cell it infects.
cards.why: A virus never divides; a host cell does the copying.
cards.quote: A bacterium copies itself; a virus is copied by a host cell.

cards.front: A virus never divides: a {{c1::host cell}}, the living cell a virus infects, does the copying.
cards.quote: A virus never divides: a host cell, the living cell a virus infects, does the copying.

cards.front: What is asexual reproduction?
cards.back: Reproduction with one parent, where the offspring get copies of that parent's DNA.
cards.quote: Asexual reproduction is reproduction with one parent, where the offspring get copies of that parent's DNA.
cards.section: Explain: how bacteria make more bacteria

cards.front: How is binary fission in a bacterium simpler than mitosis?
cards.back: A bacterium has no nucleus, so each new cell just gets a complete copy of the chromosome, the cell's main DNA, as the cell splits in two.
cards.quote: a bacterium has no nucleus, and each new cell just gets a complete copy of the chromosome, the cell's main DNA.
cards.section: Explain: how bacteria make more bacteria

cards.front: In bacteria, the DNA passed during conjugation is often a {{c1::plasmid}}, a small extra circle of DNA separate from the chromosome.
cards.quote: The DNA is often a plasmid, a small extra circle of DNA separate from the chromosome.
cards.section: Explain: how bacteria make more bacteria

cards.front: How does budding work in some bacteria?
cards.back: A small new cell grows out of the parent and then breaks off.
cards.quote: Some bacteria use budding: a small new cell grows out of the parent and then breaks off, as in the ocean bacterium below.
cards.section: Explain: how bacteria make more bacteria

cards.front: Bacterial daughter cells are usually genetically identical. How can mutations still build up in a lab E. coli population over many generations?
cards.back: Copying DNA sometimes makes mistakes, so rare changes in the DNA are passed on and accumulate across generations.
cards.quote: Copying DNA sometimes makes mistakes: sequencing studies of lab E. coli, which read the cells' DNA, found mutations (changes in the DNA) building up over many generations.
cards.section: Explain: how bacteria make more bacteria

cards.front: Why do many biologists call bacterial conjugation gene transfer rather than reproduction?
cards.back: No new cell is made. One cell passes DNA to another, so the number of cells stays the same.
cards.why: Virginia's standards call it a form of sexual reproduction because genes from two cells combine.
cards.quote: Many biologists call it gene transfer, because no new cell is made.
cards.section: Explain: how bacteria make more bacteria

cards.front: One bacterial cell passes a plasmid directly to a neighbouring cell by contact. How many cells are there before and after, and what is different about the receiving cell?
cards.back: The same number of cells, before and after. The receiving cell now carries the plasmid's genes. This is conjugation: it adds genes, not cells.
cards.quote: In conjugation, one bacterial cell passes DNA directly to another through contact.
cards.section: Explain: how bacteria make more bacteria

cards.front: {{c1::Doubling time}} is the time a population takes to double.
cards.quote: Doubling time is the time a population takes to double.
cards.section: Explain: doubling, and why it stops

cards.front: In a model population, 50 cells double every 30 minutes with no deaths, no lag and endless food. How many cells are there after 3 hours?
cards.back: 3 hours is 180 minutes, and 180 / 30 = 6 doublings. 50 x 2^6 = 50 x 64 = 3,200 cells.
cards.quote: If it stays the same, you can predict the count
cards.section: Explain: doubling, and why it stops

cards.front: In a model population doubling every 20 minutes, 800 cells grow to 6,400 cells. How long did that take?
cards.back: 800 to 1,600 to 3,200 to 6,400 is 3 doublings. 3 x 20 minutes = 60 minutes.
cards.quote: 2 hours is 120 minutes, and 120 ÷ 20 = 6 doublings.
cards.section: Explain: doubling, and why it stops

cards.front: What three assumptions does the simple doubling model make about a bacterial population?
cards.back: No cells die, there is no waiting before growth starts, and food is endless.
cards.why: Real cultures break all three, which is why real growth levels off.
cards.quote: The model assumes no cells die, no waiting before growth starts and endless food.
cards.section: Explain: doubling, and why it stops

cards.front: Constant doubling makes numbers grow very fast. Why does a real bacterial population still level off?
cards.back: Food runs out and wastes build up, so the population cannot keep doubling.
cards.quote: Constant doubling makes numbers grow very fast, but a real population levels off when food runs out and wastes build up.
cards.section: Explain: doubling, and why it stops

cards.front: In a real E. coli culture, the cloudiness barely changes at the start. What are the two possible explanations?
cards.back: A true lag, where cells are active but the count barely rises, or too few cells at the start to be seen by the machine.
cards.quote: A flat start can be a true lag or just too few cells to see.
cards.section: Elaborate: a real growth curve

cards.front: What does an OD600 reading of a liquid culture measure, and is it a cell count?
cards.back: Cloudiness: more cells scatter more light. It is not a count of cells, and even liquid with no cells reads a little cloudy.
cards.quote: It is not a count of cells, and even liquid with no cells reads a little cloudy.
cards.section: Elaborate: a real growth curve

cards.front: An E. coli well reads OD600 0.078 at the first reading, 0.134 at 8 hours and 0.198 at 10 hours. Find the rise since the first reading at 8 and 10 hours. Did it roughly double?
cards.back: Rise at 8 h: 0.134 - 0.078 = 0.056. Rise at 10 h: 0.198 - 0.078 = 0.120. 0.120 / 0.056 is about 2.1, so yes, roughly doubled in 2 hours.
cards.quote: The real rise went 0.056, 0.120, 0.235, roughly doubling every 2 hours.
cards.section: Elaborate: a real growth curve

cards.front: Why is the rise since the first OD600 reading only a rough guide to growth, not a reading of the cells alone?
cards.back: The first reading includes background cloudiness that is not from the cells, and the dataset has no cell-free well to say how much.
cards.quote: The third column subtracts the first reading: it shows the change since 0.5 hours, a rough guide to growth, not a reading of the cells alone.
cards.section: Elaborate: a real growth curve

cards.front: For the first 6 hours of a diluted E. coli culture the cloudiness hardly moved. Does that prove the cells were not dividing?
cards.back: No. After a 1,000-fold dilution the cells started far below what the machine can see, and the first several doublings are too faint to read.
cards.why: If the cells came from a culture about as cloudy as the plateau, climbing back takes about 10 doublings (2^10 = 1,024).
cards.quote: A flat start can be a true lag or just too few cells to see.
cards.section: Elaborate: a real growth curve

cards.front: From 8 to 12 hours the rise was 0.056 and then 0.235. A 20-minute doubling would give 12 doublings (x 4,096) in that time. What does the real rise show?
cards.back: The rise grew about 4-fold, not 4,096-fold: this culture did not keep a 20-minute pace from 8 to 12 hours.
cards.quote: The arithmetic shows only that this culture did not keep up a 20-minute pace from 8 to 12 hours.
cards.section: Elaborate: a real growth curve

cards.front: In a yeast sugar test, tubes with 0, 1, 2 and 4 g of sugar per 100 mL all level off at the same cloudiness. What can you conclude?
cards.back: Sugar alone did not set how far growth went. Another nutrient running out, or wastes building up, may have set the limit first.
cards.quote: If all tubes level off at the same height, something else, such as another nutrient running out or wastes building up, may set the limit first.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: You test whether sugar amount changes how high a yeast population grows. What do you measure, what stays constant and what is the control?
cards.back: Measure cloudiness every hour until readings stop rising. Keep the yeast, water volume, temperature and tubes the same. The control is the tube with no sugar.
cards.quote: Dependent variable: cloudiness every hour, using a turbidity probe or a printed card behind the tube, until the readings stop rising.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: What happens in the lytic cycle of a phage?
cards.back: The host's own machinery builds new viruses right away, and the cell often bursts to release them.
cards.quote: In the lytic cycle, the build-now-then-burst path, the host's own machinery does the copying.
cards.section: Explain: how viruses make more viruses

cards.front: In the lysogenic cycle, the stored viral DNA is called the {{c1::prophage}}.
cards.quote: In the lysogenic cycle, the carried-along path, the stored viral DNA is called the prophage.
cards.section: Explain: how viruses make more viruses

cards.front: Why can a free phage not multiply on its own?
cards.back: It takes in no food and does nothing on its own. Only inside a bacterium do the host's food, energy and machinery build new phages.
cards.quote: A free phage, a virus that infects bacteria, takes in no food and does nothing on its own.
cards.section: Explain: how viruses make more viruses

cards.front: In phage lambda, what decides whether an infection follows the lytic or the lysogenic path?
cards.back: The state of the host cell and how many phages infect it at once. It is also partly chance.
cards.quote: In phage lambda the outcome depends on the state of the host cell and on how many phages infect it at once.
cards.section: Explain: how viruses make more viruses

cards.front: A single lysogen divides for 4 rounds. Then 2 cells switch to the lytic cycle and burst. How many cells still carry the prophage?
cards.back: 14. Four rounds make 2^4 = 16 carriers, because both daughter cells get a copy at each division. Minus the 2 that burst leaves 14.
cards.quote: Either way, both daughter cells get a copy at each division.
cards.section: Explain: how viruses make more viruses

cards.front: A culture of lysogens grows in a closed well until its cloudiness levels off. What happens to the number of cells carrying the prophage?
cards.back: Roughly, it levels off too. The prophage is copied only with its host's DNA, so it meets its host's limits while cells do not switch.
cards.quote: The prophage is copied only along with its host's DNA, so while cells keep it and do not switch, it meets its host's limits.
cards.section: Explain: how viruses make more viruses

cards.front: Herpes simplex virus can sit in sensory nerve cells and later cause a new cold sore. How is this like, and unlike, lysogeny in phage lambda?
cards.back: Like: the virus hides in a living host cell and can become active again. Unlike: its DNA appears to stay as a separate circle in the nucleus, not joined to the chromosome as lambda's is.
cards.quote: Studies of infected human and mouse tissue suggest its DNA stays as a separate circle in the nucleus.
cards.section: Explain: how viruses make more viruses

cards.front: One bacterium and one phage each go through one cycle: binary fission, the lytic cycle, or the lysogenic cycle with a division. Compare what is made in each.
cards.back: Binary fission: two new cells. Lytic: many new virus particles, and the host cell dies. Lysogenic: host cells that carry viral DNA, no new viruses, and the host stays alive, unless it later switches to lytic.
cards.quote: In the lysogenic cycle it copies only the viral DNA, along with its own, each time it divides
